opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think a lot about this, because at AI Fund we work with a lot of founders who are brilliant technically but are building a company for the first time.

One thing I've found is that technical founders are often underrated as CEOs. There's a stereotype that you need a business person in charge, but especially in AI, the technology is moving so fast that the person who deeply understands what's now possible often has a real edge in making product and strategy decisions. So I don't try to turn them into someone else. I try to help them keep that technical judgment while filling in the gaps.

The gaps tend to be pretty predictable. The biggest one is going to customers early. A lot of technical people, and I've been guilty of this myself, want to build the thing first, make it really good, and then go find users. I encourage founders to get very concrete very quickly. Don't say "we're going to use AI to improve healthcare." Say "we're going to help this specific type of clinician do this specific task," and then go talk to those people and test it. A concrete idea can be validated or falsified quickly. A vague idea just feels good and never gets tested.

The second thing is speed. With generative AI and AI coding assistants, you can build a prototype in days that used to take months. So I encourage founders to build lots of quick, scrappy prototypes, put them in front of users, and throw most of them away. Engineering is getting faster, so the bottleneck is shifting to product management: figuring out what to build. Technical founders who also develop strong product instincts and user empathy do really well.

Third, I try to surround them with support so they're not learning everything the hard way: help with recruiting, go-to-market, fundraising, the operational pieces. You don't need to become an expert in all of that on day one, but you do need to know enough to hire well and make good decisions.

And finally, I tell them to be okay with not knowing things. A first-time founder is going to hit lots of situations they've never seen. The ones who succeed are the ones who learn fast, ask for help, and stay humble about what they don't know, while staying confident about the problem they're solving.

r001.rationale: The response says technical founders have an edge in technical judgment and should retain it, but also describes significant gaps in customer discovery, product management, and company operations. It does not characterize them as already possessing most of the skills needed to succeed.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So at AI Fund, we work with a lot of founders who are deeply technical, and I think the most common pattern I see is that they're great at building, but they've never had to figure out what to build. And those turn out to be very different skills.

The way I think about it, a technical founder's superpower is speed of iteration. They can take an idea and turn it into a working prototype in days. But if you point that speed at the wrong problem, you just get to the wrong answer faster. So a lot of what we do early on is slow people down, just slightly, on the question of what customer, what problem, what's the concrete validation signal, before they start writing code.

One thing I push on a lot is talking to users. It sounds obvious, but many engineers find it genuinely uncomfortable. They'd rather spend a week building a feature than spend an hour on a call that might tell them the feature isn't needed. So we try to make that a habit very early, almost like a muscle you train. Ten customer conversations before the first real sprint. It's remarkable how often the idea changes.

The second thing is helping them see that the technology is usually not the hard part anymore. With the current generation of AI tools, building a working demo is cheap. What's expensive is distribution, trust, getting a buyer inside an enterprise to say yes. Technical founders sometimes underweight that because it's not where their intuition lives. So we try to pair them with people, or at least frameworks, that cover the go-to-market side.

And then the third piece is really about pace and psychology. A lot of first-time founders are used to environments where being right matters. In a startup, being wrong quickly and cheaply matters more. So I spend time trying to lower the cost of being wrong for them. Make it okay to kill an idea after two weeks. Make it okay to pivot. Celebrate the fast failures a bit, because every one of those is information.

If I had to sum it up, I'd say the goal is to preserve what makes them great, that raw ability to build, while wrapping it in enough discipline about customers and markets that the building actually compounds into a company.

r001.rationale: The response credits technical founders with building ability and speed of iteration, but says they often lack customer discovery, market judgment, and go-to-market experience. It does not characterize them as already possessing most of the skills needed to succeed.

astra-6.text:
I think one of the biggest shifts is helping them get from thinking about what the technology can do to understanding what a customer actually needs. If you’re a strong engineer, your instinct is often to go build something. And that’s a tremendous strength. But you can spend a lot of time solving a technically interesting problem that no one urgently needs solved.

So I’d encourage a first-time founder to make the customer discovery process very concrete. Who is the user? What are they doing today? Where do they get stuck? And can you put something in front of them quickly enough to test your assumptions? Sometimes the most useful next step is writing code, and sometimes it’s having five conversations.

The other piece is giving them support in areas they haven’t had a chance to learn yet—sales, hiring, deciding which market to focus on. Being a first-time founder doesn’t mean you can’t learn those things. But having someone you can turn to with a very specific question can shorten that learning cycle considerably.

Ultimately, I want to preserve their technical ambition while helping them build a much faster feedback loop with the market.

r001.rationale: The response recognizes strong engineering as a strength but also describes sales, hiring, and market selection as areas they may still need to learn. It does not characterize these founders as already possessing most of the skills needed to succeed.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one of the biggest transitions for a highly technical founder is learning that building the technology and building a business are different jobs. You may be very good at solving a hard technical problem, but you also have to figure out: Is this a problem someone urgently needs solved? Who makes the purchasing decision? And how do you get the product into their hands?

So I would encourage a first-time founder to spend time with customers very early. And that doesn’t mean asking, “Would you use my AI product?” It means understanding what they do today, where they struggle, and what solving that problem would be worth to them. Then build something small and get it in front of them. That feedback can save you months of engineering.

The other piece is giving founders support in areas they haven’t learned yet—sales, hiring, pricing—without taking away their ownership. You want to help them make better decisions and learn faster. Technical depth is a tremendous advantage. The goal is to pair it with an equally disciplined process for discovering what customers actually want.

r001.rationale: The response identifies technical depth as an advantage but says founders must also learn customer discovery and business skills such as sales, hiring, and pricing. It does not characterize them as already possessing most of the skills needed to succeed.
